I have an ubuntu "server" with a samba share on my home network. Previously this has given me ~70MB/s real world read performance to another PC, from a secondary storage hard drive within the ubuntu PC.

Now, I'm struggling to go above 10MB/s. The router is not the bottleneck, I threw the two PCs on a switch and it is still slow.

Then I thought maybe my hard drive was having some issues since it is from ~2008 or so, so I ran:

$ sudo hdparm -t /dev/sdb1

/dev/sdb1:
 Timing buffered disk reads: 338 MB in 3.00 seconds = 112.61 MB/sec

I read hdparm isn't 100% indicative of real world speeds, but it doesn't seem to be slouching in that benchmark. So then I killed off all of my daemons that should be accessing that hard drive other than samba daemon.

My transfers are still slow, and if the drive doesn't appear to be benchmarking poorly, or to be overused by an application, or bottlenecked by network speed, then what else could it be?

Thanks!
noob question: Why is my samba share so slow suddenly?

I'm certainly not very experienced here, but has there been a recent update to your wireless/lan drivers, or to samba itself via repository? The only reason for samba to "suddenly" slow down would be a change - either user or system. If you haven't done anything, I would look to updates, and possibly look into rolling something back, depending on your findings. Sorry I wasn't much help :/

Try ethtool to tell you what network speed is being used (or use its relative,friend mii-tool)

Is it streaming at the same speed from more than one computer?

What's the client machine? I imagine you have this on a Windows network, since you're bothering with Samba? If so, there's various Windows services (remote differential compression rings a bell?) that can really toss a wrench into proper SMB traffic. All that stuff will be buried in your Windows network config, and you'll need to turn it off to do real network load testing. Also look for anything that "manages" your network traffic -- MSI is pretty bad about putting this kind of garbage on everything it ships.

If you're running a pure Unix/Linux environment, you'd be better served by moving to NFS, IMO. I know, I hate that guy on these threads, too, but it's the truth: it's faster, has less overhead, and it's far easier to configure and troubleshoot. Avoid Samba like the plague if you can get away with it.
